title: Lean practice implementation in French healthcare: a longitudinal case study.
paragraphs: Nowadays, healthcare services – and hospitals in particular – are under continuous pressure to deliver safer, faster and more patient-centred care while facing rising demand, workforce shortages and tightening financial constraints. These combined pressures have encouraged many organisations to look beyond traditional cost-cutting or bed-reduction strategies and to experiment with management approaches such as Lean and Lean Six Sigma (LSS) that promise to improve processes, reduce waste and enhance value for patients and [ 1 – 4 ].

Healthcare organisations share several characteristics with manufacturing systems – flows, queues, bottlenecks, variability and rework – which makes the transfer of Lean principles attractive. At the same time, hospitals differ in important ways: the demand is uncertain, clinical pathways are heterogeneous, and outcomes are life-critical. Over the last two decades, a large body of work has reported local Lean initiatives in emergency departments, operating theatres, laboratories and outpatient units. Systematic reviews indicate that these projects can reduce waiting times, improve patient satisfaction and cut costs. Still, they also note fragmented deployments, tool-focused implementations and mixed success when Lean is adopted at scale with generally poor sustainability of Lean long term [ 2 , 3 , 5 – 8 ].

Despite this growing literature, several gaps remain. There is limited evidence on how Lean is deployed and sustained at the hospital wide level, rather than within a single ward or service. The French context has also been comparatively under-reported, even though Lean has been progressively introduced into French hospitals over the last decade. Existing publications tend to focus either on single improvement projects or on high-level policy narratives, providing only a partial view of how Lean practices are translated into daily routines, how staff are engaged and how results are maintained over time [ 9 – 12 ]. The fact that France has one of the best healthcare systems in the world, based on access, quality, cost, and overall health of residents, and being the 3rd highest country in terms of GDP spend on healthcare at 12.1%, makes the French healthcare system a suitable and appropriate case study for this research [ 13 ]. Other Lean in healthcare research has highlighted problems with sustaining Lean once initial gains have been made, thus having a country representative of global healthcare is important for this study [ 8 ].

This study addresses these gaps by examining a longitudinal Lean deployment in a French public hospital that implemented an organisation-wide LSS programme over several years. It also explores how the hospital built internal capability, aligned Lean projects with strategic objectives and gradually shifted from isolated interventions to a more integrated, system-wide approach; all contributing to a sustainable Lean initiative as evidenced by the 5-year deployment and maintenance of progress and practices. In doing so, the paper seeks to provide an understanding of a successful Lean practice implementation in healthcare and how improvements can be sustained in a complex hospital environment. Two research questions guided the study:

Lean implementation cases in hospitals have attracted growing attention over the past two decades. McDermott et al. [ 2 , 3 ], for example, report more than 180 studies related to Lean and LSS in healthcare, signalling a sustained and expanding interest in the topic [ 7 , 14 , 15 ]. It has been shown that Lean and LSS can deliver a variety of benefits and now serve as a reference point for managers considering improvement programmes in hospitals. However, there is a severe lack of empirical case study and evidence based application of Lean in the literature [ 2 , 4 , 12 , 16 ]. Benefits of Lean in healthcare include reduced costs and better use of resources [ 17 , 18 ], shorter waiting times [ 19 ] and redesigned processes that support more patient-centred care [ 4 , 20 ].

Mapping and analysing patient pathways is seen as a key step in eliminating waste and improving health-delivery processes [ 21 ], as well as in redesigning clinical processes to improve outcomes [ 1 , 22 ]. Empirical studies report reductions in errors and inappropriate procedures when Lean is applied with careful attention to organisational and mindset change [ 2 , 11 ]. Stentoft and Freytag [ 23 ] stress that the importance of cultivating an “improvement culture” that goes beyond cost-cutting to focus on process quality, responsiveness and reliability of care [ 24 ], while also improving safety and reducing the unnecessary length of stay for patients [ 25 ].

The literature highlights limitations and challenges. Radnor et al. [ 26 ] show that Lean application in healthcare ranges from the use of isolated tools to attempts at transformational, organisation-wide programmes combining bottom-up participation with top-down direction [ 27 ]. Many initiatives have been judged to make only limited use of the quality improvement and Lean toolbox, even though case studies describe a broad range of tools such as process mapping, value stream mapping, 5 S, PDCA, Kaizen, spaghetti charts, Ishikawa diagrams, hazard analysis, Gemba walks, A3 reports, brainstorming, Heijunka, process indicators (e.g. cycle time, takt time), kata, voice of the customer and Hoshin Kanri [ 2 , 3 ]. Visual tools such as VSM and process mapping are widely used to clarify flows when data are ambiguous [ 28 ].

The context in which Lean is deployed adds further complexity. Hospitals as they operate in a service setting, must deal with emergencies, fluctuating demand and capacity constraints while managing clinical risk and regulatory requirements [ 2 ]. These features make implementation more challenging than in many industrial settings and demand a nuanced understanding of how Lean interacts within healthcare complexity [ 29 ]. Leadership support is a critical driver in creating an environment that supports problem-solving and continuous improvement [ 12 , 30 ].

Authors [ 9 , 10 ] argue that there is a need to move beyond descriptive accounts of tools towards studies that explore how Lean is actually introduced, governed and adapted in hospitals. Curatolo et al. [ 5 ] found that around 59% of Lean healthcare articles mainly describe the content of implementation approaches, often with relatively low methodological maturity, while other studies focus on engineering details of specific processes. Systematic reviews of LSS applications confirm that the published literature is dominated by projects in individual departments – such as outpatient clinics [ 12 ], hospital pharmacies [ 7 ], primary care units [ 31 ], and diagnostic imaging processes [ 32 ] – rather than by organisation-wide programmes [ 2 , 3 , 6 ].

Taken together, these reviews point to important gaps. There is still limited understanding of how Lean is deployed and sustained at the whole-hospital level, how clinical and support services are connected within a coherent Lean system, and how results are sustained over time. There is also a recognised need for structured, empirically grounded guidance for managers on how to plan, phase and steer Lean deployment in healthcare [ 5 , 33 , 34 ]. Rosa et al. [ 12 ], emphasise that the implementation process itself – including issues of context, governance and long-term sustainability – remains under-investigated. The present study responds to these calls by examining a longitudinal, organisation-wide Lean programme in a French public hospital and by exploring the drivers that supported its implementation and maintenance.

The study employs a qualitative, longitudinal single-case study design. The case was purposefully selected because it offered: (i) a multi-year Lean deployment across several services; (ii) access to key informants directly involved in leading the programme; and (iii) rich documentation and performance data that allowed longitudinal analysis [ 35 ]. In line with this logic, the research focuses on a single public French hospital and follows its organisation-wide LSS programme over several years.

Francesatto et al. [ 36 ] argue that detailed case studies are fundamental for understanding how LSS is actually deployed, the difficulties encountered, and the critical success factors that emerge in real organisational settings. Padadopoulos [ 22 ] highlight the usefulness of qualitative case studies for tracing actors, decisions and outcomes in complex healthcare processes.

The case site, referred to as “Greta Hospital” for confidentiality, is a large public teaching hospital in France. Greta has approximately 2,000 beds and 8,000 staff and is recognised as one of the leading trauma centres in the country. The hospital launched a Lean management approach to address a substantial financial deficit and improve quality and patient flow. It was an early adopter of Lean in the French healthcare system and implemented an organisation-wide programme covering core clinical and support services.

The COREQ is a qualitative research methodology that aids in reporting and replicating qualitative research in a clear manner [ 37 ]. We followed COREQ’s key steps as follows in Table 1 , and within each step, adhered to a 32-item checklist to ensure each core step was followed.

Ethical considerations were carefully addressed. The hospital is anonymised as “Greta”, and no patient-identifiable information is reported. Interviewees participated voluntarily, and their views are presented in aggregate to protect confidentiality. Ethics approval was not required by the research institutions where the study was carried out, as no patient health data was used, nor were any employees involved in the study under 18 or vulnerable.

Prior to the study, an information session was held outlining the study’s purpose and its focus on action research of hospital processes as part of Step 1 of the CoreQ methodological approach. As per the correct study design, the study was carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki principles, and all participants provided informed consent to be observed and to participate in information interviews, focus groups, and brainstorming sessions.

In total, over 100 interviews were carried out pre- and post-study with anyone involved in the Lean program within the hospital. Focus groups were primarily utilised because they enabled a wide variety of opinions and ideas to be discussed simultaneously. Focus groups generally took place over a 1–2 h period, while one-to-one interviews required a 30-minute time slot. Researchers also observed how Kaizens and Lean team meetings and daily “huddles” were conducted in an effort to understand Lean workings in Greta.

Pre-interviews prior to Lean program implementation consisted of 3 high-level questions asking (1) What works well in your process area and why?, (2) What doesn’t work well and why, and (3) What would you like to see improved?. Post-change Lean implementation, there were also interviews consisting of high-level questions such as “Has the improvement worked and if so, why?” and “Do you see further opportunity for improvement?”. These questions formed the thematic areas and coding areas later post the interviews.

Multiple in-depth and follow-up interviews and informal discussions were conducted with the Lean program manager to inform to reconstruct the programme’s chronology, understand the rationale for key decisions, and clarify how specific Lean projects were selected and executed. In addition, interviews and conversations were held with clinicians, nurses and managers involved in Lean projects in the operating room, the sterilisation service department, the Sortology unit, the biology and genetic laboratories, and inter-service redeployment. These interviews were complemented by non-documentary sources formed a second major pillar of the evidence base. Internal presentation slides, project charters, implementation plans, training materials and performance dashboards were collected and analysed. These documents included, for example, process maps, value stream maps, indicator definitions, before-and-after performance data and internal reports summarising project outcomes. They provided factual information on volumes, waiting times, non-conformities and financial performance, as well as insight into how Lean concepts were communicated inside the hospital.

Data analysis followed an iterative, inductive–deductive process typical of qualitative case research [ 38 , 39 ]. First, interview notes and documents were organised chronologically to construct a narrative of Lean deployment at Greta Hospital. A mix of Microsoft Excel and Atlas qualitative analysis software was used to collate interview results under different thematic codes and areas, e.g., problems, areas of potential improvement, what works well, and what did not work well. Separate within-case narratives were developed for each major service (e.g., operating room, sterilisation, Sortology, laboratories), capturing initial conditions, Lean interventions, local adaptations and observed outcomes. Second, these narratives were coded to identify recurring themes related to leadership, patient focus, team composition, pacing of implementation and mechanisms for maintaining contact with the field. In this stage, attention was paid to both local specificities and cross-cutting patterns. The methods of open coding, focused and theoretical coding methods were applied [ 40 ]. A systematic analytic process, including comparison and researcher member-checking, was adopted to enhance credibility [ 41 ]. Third, emergent themes were compared with the existing literature on Lean healthcare and LSS implementation [ 22 , 36 , 42 ] through pattern matching. This led to the formulation of the five drivers of Lean deployment that are presented and discussed in Section “ Discussion: Acknowledging the key drivers to sustain Lean healthcare ”.

Several steps were taken to enhance the rigour and trustworthiness of the study. Methodological triangulation was used by combining interviews, observations and documentary analysis [ 43 ]. Data source triangulation was achieved by drawing on multiple informants from different professional groups and hierarchical levels. A chain of evidence was maintained by linking raw data, intermediate analyses and final interpretations, and by systematically recording decisions made during the analytic process [ 39 ].

This section describes how Lean and LSS were deployed across Greta Hospital’s core clinical and support processes (RQ1). Based on the interviews, data review, and action research, we have detailed individual projects and identified problem areas, and how these areas were improved utilising Lean methods. We focus on five flagship implementation areas: the operating room (OR), the sterilisation service department (SSD), the discharge coordination “Sortology” unit, the biology and genetic laboratories, and inter-service staff redeployment. These areas were the flagship areas of the Lean program from their initiation over 5 years ago to currently being sustained in ongoing Lean and continuous improvement since then. For each area, we outline the initial problem, the main Lean interventions and the key performance outcomes, laying the groundwork for the analysis of Lean deployment drivers in Section “ Discussion: Acknowledging the key drivers to sustain Lean healthcare ” to answer RQ2.

The first major Lean initiative at Greta Hospital was launched in the operating room, a critical area for both patient outcomes and hospital finances. Early Gemba visits and simple indicators showed that OR capacity was being underused. Although surgeons and anaesthetists routinely arrived before 7:00 a.m., the first operation of the day rarely started on time. The “Hour of First Incision” (HFI) indicator, which records the time of the first surgical incision for each team, revealed systematic delays. Late starts compressed the daily schedule, increased cancellations and created pressure on staff and downstream services.

A cross-functional team involving the OR chief nurse, surgeons, anaesthetists and support staff was created to address this problem. The initial focus was on making performance visible. A whiteboard displayed the planned schedule and the actual HFIs for each operating list, while staff noted any incidents that contributed to delays. After several weeks, this simple device provided a clear picture of typical start times and recurring issues, and served as a shared factual basis for discussion.

Using basic problem-solving tools, including Pareto analysis, the team identified a small number of dominant causes: patients arriving late or incompletely prepared; missing or delayed sterile instruments and consumables; unfinished cleaning tasks; and the late arrival of some physicians. Many of these issues originated outside the OR, in upstream wards, the sterilisation department and housekeeping. The team prioritised those causes with the greatest impact on HFI and that could be tackled quickly.

Following Lean principle, admission rules were tightened so that all patients scheduled for morning surgery arrived and were prepared before a fixed cut-off time. Standard work was introduced for pre-operative preparation and room set-up, with clear responsibilities for checking instruments and supplies. Visual controls helped staff spot missing items earlier, and an Andon-type signal alerted the chief nurse when a problem risked delaying the list. Short daily huddles reviewed the previous day’s HFIs and agreed on immediate corrective actions, supported by follow-up calls with surgeons when chronic delays were observed.

Within a year, the average HFI moved closer to the planned start time and variability in first incisions reduced. More reliable starts and fewer cancellations generated an estimated 30% increase in effective OR capacity. The results have been sustained via daily and weekly core Lean routines; the implementation of transparent performance measurements (key performance indicators), maintaining a multidisciplinary problem-solving team and a focus on system-wide causes of delay rather than on individual blame.

The Sterilisation Service Department (SSD) is responsible for cleaning, disinfecting, sterilising and redistributing medical disposables and surgical instruments to the operating rooms and more than 100 care units. When the Lean deployment began, the SSD was a major constraint for Greta Hospital. Sterilised equipment sets were frequently incomplete or incorrect when they arrived in the OR, forcing last-minute re-sterilisation, delaying operations, and effectively reducing the hospital’s treatment capacity. Internal indicators, including the IAD performance measure, showed high variability and recurrent non-conformities in the flow of medical disposables. A small multidisciplinary team was formed, involving SSD staff, OR nurses and pharmacy technicians. The group first mapped the existing flow of medical disposables from the OR back to the SSD and then forward again to the clinical units. This “before” situation, was a complex, fragmented pathway with multiple handovers, re-sorting steps and unclear responsibilities. Instruments and disposables from different procedures were often mixed, and the SSD had to spend time reconstructing sets with limited information about their composition or urgency.

The first improvement focused on the point of use. A simple checklist and standard document indicated which items belonged together and how they should be arranged. This pre-sorting task took only a few minutes but ensured items arrived at the SSD in a more organised state, reducing the risk of mixing and loss and making it easier for SSD staff to recognise and process complete sets.

Subsequent changes targeted the SSD’s internal workflow. The team redesigned the physical layout and process sequence to create a clearer, more linear pathway. Workstations were reorganised so that cleaning, inspection, packaging and sterilisation followed each other without unnecessary backtracking. Visual management was introduced to control work-in-progress (WIP): WIP areas were marked on the floor and divided into zones indicating normal, high, and critical load. When stock reached a warning zone, staff could be reassigned or additional help requested to prevent bottlenecks. Standard work defined the sequence of tasks for each role, improving synchronisation between cleaning and sterilisation activities.

These changes stabilised the SSD’s performance. The variability of the IAD indicator fell by about 50%, the rate of quality non-conformities decreased by roughly 30%, and overall SSD capacity increased, allowing it to supply around 98% of medical disposables in a ready-to-use condition. In addition to these measurable results, the SSD project reinforced collaboration between OR and support services. It demonstrated that relatively simple Lean interventions at the departmental interface could unlock significant system-wide benefits. As mentioned in the OR section; sustaining of results is important; a Lean team is in place in the SSD, key performance indicators are reviewed daily and weekly and Lean actions and continuous improvement projects are worked on over time to ensure patient focus.

Greta Hospital faced a chronic shortage of beds. There was no possibility of transferring patients to another facility within 100 km, so new admissions sometimes had to be placed in spare beds in the corridors. These “corridor beds” created obvious problems: lack of oxygen points, poor thermal comfort, limited privacy, increased infection risk and difficult working conditions for staff. A simple measurement exercise showed that, on average, 18 patients per month were being treated in corridor beds.

A first Gemba exercise started by walking through the wards, and a geriatrician and the quality director examined why so many rooms remained occupied. They identified more than 100 inpatients with “medical–social” problems who were still in beds although acute treatment was essentially complete. Some had complex, multi-pathology conditions requiring multiple specialists and coordination that residential care homes could not easily absorb. Others stayed because of social issues: no available caregiver, inability to live independently, or no place yet secured in a nursing home.

The hospital benchmarked UK hospitals on bed planning and discharge coordination, and launched an innovative project called the “Sortology unit” which treated complex discharge planning as a dedicated process rather than leaving to already-overloaded ward teams.

The Sortology unit applied core Lean principles to the discharge process. A pull logic was introduced: instead of asking, “Who can we admit?“, the team asked, “Which patients can we safely and sustainably discharge to free beds for those waiting?“. Once a week, typically on Thursday, the quality director, social assistant and chief nurse met for about 45 min around this board. They reviewed each case, coordinated with city medical and social services, and, when necessary, triggered a rapid trusteeship procedure through a medical examiner to clarify legal responsibility and obtain signatures within 48 h. The aim was to achieve at least one complex discharge per meeting and to reassure patients and families that support would continue after leaving the hospital, with the option of readmission if problems arose. In Lean terms, the Sortology unit combined pull (regulated discharge flow), Jidoka (ensuring safe conditions before leaving), empowerment (front-line decision-making) and “reusable knowledge” by learning from each unique case and applying that learning to subsequent discharges.

The Sortology unit helped smooth the flow of departing patients, particularly those coming from the emergency department, which accounted for around 80% of potential complex discharges. Length of stay for targeted patients dropped by about 18%, with roughly 75% of admissions meeting acceptable length-of-stay targets and only 25% remaining above them. The use of corridor beds was significantly reduced, and after about 18 months the hospital created an additional social worker post to sustain and extend this approach. In practice, the Sortology unit acted as an interface between hospital services and community providers, using Lean thinking to release blocked capacity while maintaining safe, patient-centred discharges.

The results of the Lean Sortology project are sustained as previously mentioned via review of key performance measures e.g., length of stay and staff work on ongoing Lean projects to maintain and improve service level (see Table 2 ).

The biology laboratory performs more than 80% of the hospital’s analyses. At the start of the Lean journey, a recurrent and stressful problem was the shortage of critical reagents. Stockouts triggered urgent orders, delayed vital tests and created anxiety for staff who knew that some patients could not safely wait. The challenge was to secure a reliable flow of reagents without building excessive inventory.

To address this, the team designed a simple pull system using Kanban. For each key reagent, two bins were installed: the front bin for current use and a second bin behind it to trigger replenishment. When the first bin was empty, staff were supposed to move to the second bin and place a Kanban signal so that the replenisher could order a new batch. In practice, however, many different users accessed the reagents and often drew from both bins in parallel, causing the system to fail. The Lean team therefore added an error-prevention (Poka Yoke) element: the second bin was sealed with tape holding the Kanban card. To access the backup stock, staff had to break the tape, remove the card and place it in a visible collection point that automatically initiated the order. This prevented silent use of the second bin and ensured that consumption always generated a replenishment signal.

The solution required only brief training (one biologist and two agents) but proved highly robust. Over the following four years, no reagent shortages were recorded for the items covered by the system. The Kanban with Poka Yoke stabilised the ordering cycle, reduced mental workload for laboratory staff and avoided last-minute crises that had previously affected the entire hospital. The Biology lab has maintained its own Lean team as have other areas to drive and focus on continuous improvement. The key performance indicators are reviewed on a daily and weekly basis to decide focus actions to sustain improvement.

A recurring challenge at Greta Hospital was the uneven distribution of workload across services. On the same day, one ward could be operating at or beyond capacity, with nurses struggling to keep up with basic care, while another ward had spare beds and staff with available time. This imbalance created Muri (overburden) in busy services, undermined the quality of care and staff morale, and limited the hospital’s ability to respond to peaks in emergency admissions.

To tackle this, the Lean team and nursing management worked together to design a simple mechanism for resource “elasticity” across the hospital. Each unit reported a small set of indicators daily, such as occupied beds, patient dependency, and expected admissions or discharges. These data were consolidated into a visual overview that made differences in workload immediately apparent. On this basis, short coordination meetings – often combined with existing morning huddles – were held to decide where temporary support was needed and which teams could safely release one or two staff members for part of a shift.

Inter-service deployment was implemented gradually. Initially, a limited number of wards agreed to participate, and staff movements were restricted to short periods and clearly defined tasks. Nurses and healthcare assistants received basic cross-training so that they could be effective when working outside their home ward while still respecting professional boundaries and patient safety. Criteria were established to trigger support (for example, when occupancy and dependency exceeded agreed thresholds). The Lean coordinator helped mediate requests, ensuring that no unit acted solely as a “donor” or a “receiver”.

Over time, this flexible deployment system improved the hospital’s capacity to absorb fluctuations in demand without resorting systematically to overtime or agency staff. Peak workloads were shared more evenly, reducing stress in the most pressured wards and improving nurse-to-patient ratios at critical moments. Just as importantly, inter-services deployment reinforced a hospital-wide perspective: staff began to see themselves as part of a single care system rather than isolated units competing for resources. As mentioned in all of the previous focus areas, sustainment of these results is achieved by ensuring staff have the time to work on Lean projects and improving key performance indicators.

Adopting a strategy for Lean deployment and ensuring that appropriate resources are in place were key to sustaining this Lean program which is now in place over 5 years. Staff are allocated time to work on projects and key performance metrics allow progress to be measured, maintained and sustained.

This study set out to understand how Lean was introduced, implemented and sustained in a French public hospital with a particular focus on key areas of deployment (RQ1), which were outlined in Section “ Results of Lean implementation in Greta hospital ” and to identify the organisational and contextual drivers that supported this transformation (RQ2). Over five years, Greta Hospital moved from isolated improvement initiatives to a more integrated Lean system spanning core clinical and support services. Lean deployment in the OR project improved first-incision times and effective theatre capacity; the SSD work stabilised the flow of sterile instruments; the Sortology unit unlocked blocked beds by tackling complex discharges; and the biology and genetic laboratories reduced stockouts and strengthened built-in quality. Taken together, these initiatives illustrate how Lean can be used not only to improve local processes but also to reshape patient flows and resource use across the entire hospital (RQ1).

Figure 1 synthesises these observations in the form of five interdependent success drivers: hospital direction commitment (D.1), patient focus (D.2), team composition and project portfolio (D.3), step-by-step conversions (D.4) and remaining close to the field (D.5) that drive organisational deployment of Lean (RQ2). Rather than treating these drivers as a checklist, the case suggests that it is their combined effect over time that explains both the depth and durability of Lean implementation (RQ2). These findings align with similar studies by Rosa et al. [ 12 ] who in their longitudinal study of Lean deployment in Apulia over 5 years described the importance of senior management and government funding commitment to Lean success as well as a key focus on employee involvement, patient focus and incremental improvements area by area. Table 3 links these drivers to concrete practices observed at Greta, while Table 4 summarises how they played out across the programme’s different phases.

Several drivers of sustainable Lean deployment were identified in answer to RQ1 and RQ2 following on from the interviews, the focus groups and by documenting the Lean deployment in the key areas in the hospital and looking at the performance improvement. Many authors have discussed the difficulties and barriers to sustaining Lean in healthcare particularly on a long term basis, after early high engagement and quick wins [ 8 , 12 , 44 ]. The following are the key drivers that emerged over time of Lean implementation in the case study hospital. These drivers align somewhat with Rosa et al.’s [ 12 ] learnings from their longitudinal Apulian case study and with Van-Zyl Cillie et al.’s [ 8 ] proposition that hospitals “prepare, plan, experiment and learn and sustain”.

The first driver concerns visible and sustained commitment from the hospital’s top management. At Greta, Lean was not framed as a short-term cost-cutting campaign but as a strategic approach to address both financial deficits and patient flow problems. The hospital director and senior team management explicitly endorsed Lean projects, allocated time for staff to participate, and accepted that some initiatives would challenge existing organisational boundaries [ 45 ]. Leadership commitment was evidenced in the decision to appoint a Quality/Performance Director with a clear mandate to lead Lean, and by the willingness to experiment with novel arrangements such as the Sortology unit, and in the readiness to invest in additional capacity (e.g., an extra social worker) when early results were promising. This aligns with previous studies that highlight leadership as a critical success factor in Lean healthcare [ 12 , 26 ].

Second, the case reinforces the centrality of patient focus as a guiding principle for Lean in hospitals. In line with the literature that defines value from the patient’s perspective [ 46 ], projects at Greta were consistently selected and framed around patient-relevant problems rather than solely on internal efficiency. The OR work targeted delayed first incisions and cancellations; the SSD project aimed to ensure that surgical sets and disposables arrived complete and ready to use; the Sortology unit sought to eliminate the indignity and risk of corridor beds by shortening and securing discharge for complex patients. Table 2 shows how patient-centred and staff-centred indicators were used together, emphasising safety, waiting times, continuity of care and workload. By anchoring Lean goals to deliver patient service the hospital increased engagement and made it easier to sustain gains beyond the initial project period.

A third driver concerns the composition of improvement teams and the construction of the project portfolio. At Greta, Lean projects were rarely confined to a single professional group. Teams typically brought together physicians, nurses, healthcare assistants, SSD technicians, social workers and managers. This cross-professional design helped to remove silos and increase team work [ 3 ]. For example, the SSD initiative could not have succeeded without OR nurses taking responsibility for pre-sorting, and the Sortology unit relied on the joint work of clinicians, social workers and administrative staff. The Quality/Performance Director played a bridging role, connecting services and ensuring that local projects complemented rather than contradicted one another. Table 3 illustrates how this cross-functional approach was reflected across the project portfolio. Rather than launching many small, uncoordinated initiatives, the hospital focused on a limited number of high-impact processes that together shaped patient flow and capacity. This resonates with calls in the literature for more strategic alignment of Lean projects in healthcare [ 2 , 10 ].

The fourth driver concerns the pace and sequencing of Lean deployment. Greta did not attempt a “big bang” transformation. Instead, Lean was introduced through a series of step-by-step deployments that when aggregated helped extend the Lean program and scope. This mirrored the lessons of Van-Zyl Cillie [ 8 ] who talked about “experimenting and learning” with projects and area deployment before achieving sustained long-term culture and progress. Early projects, such as the OR HFI initiative and the kanban system for reagents, were relatively contained and focused on making performance visible, stabilising processes and demonstrating tangible benefits. These enabled more complex interventions that required organisational redesign, such as the new SSD flow and the creation of the Sortology unit were easier to garner support for. Rosa et al. [ 12 ] discussed the importance of sharing successes and improvements in different areas so that others could see the benefits in terms of reduced waste, administration and workload. This phased approach allowed staff to learn Lean routines gradually and adapt tools to the hospital context [ 47 ].

The final driver emphasises the importance of staying close to day-to-day work (or Gemba). Throughout the programme, managers and the Quality/Performance Director made regular Gemba visits to wards, SSD, laboratories and the emergency department. Problems were discussed in situ, using visual boards and simple indicators, rather than in distant offices. Weekly or daily huddles – for example, the Thursday Sortology meetings or the short OR reviews of first incisions – created short feedback loops between strategy and practice were crucial for sustaining Lean [ 12 ]. In this way, Lean was not reduced to a set of tools or a project methodology, but became a way of continuously confronting organisational assumptions with field reality. This echoes arguments that successful Lean healthcare requires an “improvement culture” rooted in everyday problem-solving [ 23 , 30 ], and the Greta case offers concrete examples of how such a culture can be sustained over time [ 44 ].

The findings provide several contributions to the Lean healthcare literature. First, the study integrates dispersed insights on critical success factors into a coherent set of five drivers, grounded in a longitudinal, organisation-wide case. Previous reviews have catalogued tools, benefits and challenges [ 2 , 6 , 27 ], but often treat drivers such as leadership, culture and patient focus separately. This case shows how direction commitment, patient orientation, cross-functional team design, phased implementation and proximity to the field work together as an interacting system, rather than as isolated elements.

Second, the study offers a process view of Lean deployment in a hospital context. By following Greta over several years and across multiple services, it moves beyond the single-project perspective that dominates much of the published work [ 5 , 7 ]. Figure 1 ; Tables 3 and 4 make explicit how Lean capabilities accumulate over time: local improvements in OR and laboratory processes created confidence and expertise that later supported more ambitious redesign in SSD and discharge coordination. Correlating with Van-Zyn-Cillie et al.’s [ 8 ] focus on experimentation and not being afraid to fail, the study shows the importance of selecting areas for “quick wins” and communicating early successes, and embedding the methods in smaller areas before tacking more ambitious complex projects [ 12 ]. This temporal lens helps explain why some hospitals struggle to “scale up” Lean and highlights the importance of sequencing and learning.

Third, the case adds evidence from a French public hospital, a context that has received relatively little attention compared with US and UK based healthcare systems. The establishment of the Sortology unit, in particular, demonstrates how Lean principles can be used to bridge hospital and community services in addressing complex “medical–social” cases. In this way, the study broadens understanding of how Lean interacts with different institutional environments.

It is important that Lean initiatives in healthcare don’t make the mistakes and fall down due to common barriers, as identified by Kunnen et al. [ 44 ] in sustaining Lean including overburdening employees with responsibilities, omitting staff involvement during Lean implementation, lack of patient engagement, lack of resources to engage with Lean, a lack of leadership commitment and follow-up on projects, and a lack of knowledge of Lean among leaders. This hospital ensured these barriers were minimised via the following steps:

Visible and consistent Leadership; Lean was made a core part of the hospital’s management system, a lean leader with a mandate was deployed and projects were aligned with recognised pain points in patient flow and safety.

Project teams need to be genuinely cross-functional, with sufficient autonomy to change processes that cross departmental lines. Assigning a bridging role to a quality or project function can help coordinate the project portfolio and avoid fragmentation.

Managers should avoid the temptation to launch too many initiatives at once. A phased approach that begins with a few strategically chosen processes, consolidates gains, and then extends Lean principles to connected areas appears more realistic and sustainable.

Having mechanisms to stay close to the field – regular Gemba walks, structured huddles around visual boards and open channels for staff to raise issues – are critical to keep Lean alive beyond the initial launch. Without these tools, they risk becoming static and disconnected from daily work.

For policymakers and healthcare authorities, the Greta experience underscores the value of supporting hospitals not only in acquiring Lean tools but also in developing the organisational conditions captured by the five drivers. These findings reinforce those of Rosa et al. [ 12 ] who demonstrated that the support and leadership provided by Apulian health authorities in Italy over a 5-year period were integral to sustaining the Lean program, ensuring that gains were not just in the short term.

The case contributes to ongoing debates about how best to promote operational excellence in public healthcare systems, suggesting that Lean can be a powerful lever when embedded in a coherent, long-term strategy rather than applied as a series of disconnected projects.

This study examined how Lean was introduced, implemented, and sustained in a French public hospital over several years and identified the key organisational and contextual drivers that supported this journey (RQ1 and RQ2). By following Greta Hospital’s Lean programme across core clinical and support services – the operating room, sterilisation, discharge coordination and laboratories – the study showed how local projects can gradually evolve into a more integrated hospital-wide Lean system (Q1). The results are sustained and can be sustained via the five interdependent drivers that underpinned this transformation. These are hospital direction commitment, patient focus, team composition and project portfolio, step-by-step conversions and remaining close to the Gemba. Rather than treating these as isolated success factors, the case shows how they reinforce one another over time.

A phased implementation allowed capabilities to build gradually, while regular Gemba visits and huddles kept Lean grounded in day-to-day reality. Together, these elements offer a process-based explanation for how Lean can move beyond pilot projects to become part of a hospital’s management system.

As with any single-case study, the research has limitations. The analysis is based on one hospital and on a reconstruction of its Lean journey, drawing on interviews, observations and internal documentation. Caution is therefore needed in generalising the findings directly to other settings, but the learnings over a 5-year period can inform how to sustain and deploy other Lean initiatives.

Future research could extend this work in several directions. Comparative studies across multiple hospitals and health systems would help to test and refine the five drivers identified here and to explore how they interact with different institutional arrangements and funding models.

Formal ethical approval by an IRB was not required, as under the procedures of the researchers’ respective institutions (University of Galway (1) and University of Bordeaux (2)); (1) “formal ethics review board approval is only required if your research involves minors or vulnerable participants, or you are conducting health research, e.g., the use of patient data, or data is being utilised as part of a clinical trial. (2) The research teams at the University of Bordeaux carry out research on human subjects that do not fall within the remit of French Ethics Committees (Comités de protection des personnes - CPP). As they do not aim to “develop biological or medical knowledge”, it is not considered “research involving human subjects” (RIPH) within the meaning of the Jardé Law. Informed consent to participate in this action research study on hospital processes was obtained from all employees involved. The study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and ethical standards.
